You say how you feel and where you are. You learn the difference between SER and ESTAR.
To say how you feel: tired, happy, ill, busy.
To say where you are and ask where someone else is.
To use the verb ESTAR with every person.
To choose correctly between SER and ESTAR (the big problem for beginners!).
To make the adjective agree with the person: cansado / cansada.
The next day, Ana calls Mihai.
Hi, Ana! I’m a little tired. And you?
I’m very happy. I’m not working today.
How nice! Where are you now?
I’m at home. And you? Are you at the hotel?
No, I’m not at the hotel. I’m at the Prado Museum.
Yes, I’m alone. My friend Andrei is ill. He’s at the hotel.
In Spanish B and V are pronounced THE SAME, like a soft “b”. “Vale” sounds like “bale”. Between vowels the lips barely touch.
D between vowels (and at the end) is very soft, almost like the “th” in English “this”: cansado → “cansa-tho”. At the end it is barely heard: Madrid.
The groups ie and ue are read as one quick syllable: bien = “byen” (not “bi-en”), bueno = “bwe-no”.
English has a single verb “to be”. Spanish has TWO: SER (you learned it in chapter 1) and ESTAR. Both translate as “to be”, but they are used in different situations.
Notice the accents: estás, está, estáis, están. Without the accent, “esta” means “this”, which is something else!
2. SER or ESTAR? The rule made simple
Think of it like this: SER says WHAT someone or something is, things that belong to identity. ESTAR says HOW it is right now and WHERE it is.
ESTAR: how / where it is now
Memory trick: if you can ask “HOW do you FEEL?” or “WHERE are you?”, use ESTAR. ESTAR sounds like “STATE”: estar = the state you are in.
Ana is from Madrid (her origin, SER).
Ana is in Madrid (where she is now, ESTAR).
The classic mistake: “Soy cansado”. Correct: “Estoy cansado”. Tiredness is a state, not your identity.
For the PLACE where something is, always use ESTAR, even if it’s permanent: “Madrid está en España.”
Spanish adjectives change depending on who is speaking. A man says “estoy cansado”, a woman says “estoy cansada”. English doesn’t do this, so it needs practice.
Adjectives ending in -e (triste, libre, grave) have the same form for men and women.
If you are a woman, always say “estoy cansada, contenta, ocupada, enferma, sola”. Most beginners forget and speak in the masculine.
“En” means both “in” and “at” when you say where something is: en casa (at home), en el hotel (at the hotel), en Madrid (in Madrid).
My friend is at the hotel.
“En casa” = at home (without an article), just like English “at home”, not “at the home”.
To “¿Cómo estás?” you answer with ESTAR: “Estoy bien / mal / regular”. Or simply: “Bien, gracias”.
State = ESTAR, and a woman uses -a.
El hotel es en el centro.
El hotel está en el centro.
Someone tells you they are ill. What do you say?
My friend is at the hotel.
Soy de Rumanía y estoy en Madrid.
Estoy de Rumanía y soy en Madrid.
Un domingo en el parque del Retiro
On Sunday, Madrid’s Retiro Park is full of people. Each one is different.
Today is Sunday and it’s sunny. Retiro Park is full of people.
Ana and Mihai are on a bench, next to the lake.
Ana is very happy because she isn’t working today.
Mihai is calm, but a little tired.
Next to them there is a child. The child is sad because his dog isn’t there.
Where is the dog? It’s behind a tree!
Now the child is very happy.
On another bench there is a girl. She is nervous because she has an exam tomorrow.
Her boyfriend is bored: the girl’s book is very long.
Andrei, Mihai’s friend, isn’t in the park. He’s still ill, at the hotel.
Mihai says: “Andrei is alone. Are you free at six? Let’s go to the hotel.”
Ana answers: “Of course! That way Andrei won’t be alone.”
Andrei is Mihai’s friend. He is from Romania and he is an engineer.
He’s in Madrid now, on holiday, but today he isn’t well.
He’s in bed at the hotel. He’s very tired and a little sad.
Mihai isn’t with him: he’s at the museum with Ana.
In the afternoon, Mihai calls: “How are you, Andrei?”.
“So-so. I’m better, but I’m still ill,” Andrei answers.
In the evening, Mihai and Ana are at the hotel with a hot soup.
